cards.f: Which field controls whether the agentic loop continues or ends?
cards.b: stop_reason. Continues while it is tool_use, ends on end_turn. Never parse natural language, and never use an iteration cap as the primary criterion.

cards.f: With which role do tool results return to the conversation?
cards.b: With role: user, in tool_result blocks linked by tool_use_id. There is no tool or function role in the Claude API.

cards.f: Two tool_result formatting rules that return 400 if broken
cards.b:
1) The message goes immediately after the assistant that emitted the tool_use.
2) tool_result blocks go first in the content array; text after them.

cards.f: A tool fails. How do you tell the model?
cards.b: A tool_result with is_error: true and a readable cause. It is not an exception in your app: it is information so the agent can correct course.

cards.f: The four values of tool_choice
cards.b: auto (default with tools) · any (some tool) · tool (a specific one) · none (default without tools).

cards.f: Side effect of forcing tool_choice to any or tool
cards.b: The API prefills the assistant turn, so there will be no natural text before the tool_use.

cards.f: What is the most important factor in a tool's performance?
cards.b: The description. Literally in the docs: «by far the most important factor». Target: at least 3-4 sentences. Rewriting them cut completion time by 40% in Anthropic's tests.

cards.f: At how many tools does model selection start to degrade?
cards.b: 30-50 tools available. The fix is consolidating operations into fewer tools and using tool search. Splitting them across several MCP servers does not help: the model still sees the total.

cards.f: Client tools vs server tools
cards.b:
Client: stop_reason: tool_use arrives, you run them and return the result.
Server: Anthropic runs them inside the same request (web search, code execution, MCP connector).

cards.f: What does a subagent inherit from the parent's context?
cards.b: Nothing from the history. Only the prompt string it is invoked with crosses over, plus its own system prompt, the project's CLAUDE.md and the tool definitions.

cards.f: What does a subagent return to the coordinator?
cards.b: Only its final message, as a tool result. It may have spent tens of thousands of tokens and return a distillate of 1,000-2,000 tokens.

cards.f: How do you launch several subagents in parallel?
cards.b: By emitting several spawn calls in a single response from the coordinator. One per turn is sequential execution in disguise.

cards.f: The coordinator cannot invoke subagents. What do you check first?
cards.b: That the spawn tool is in allowedTools. Without that, it falls through to the permission callback or is denied.

cards.f: Why route all communication through the coordinator?
cards.b: For observability, consistent error handling and control of information flow. Not for savings: multi-agent setups consume ~15× the tokens of a chat.

cards.f: Token consumption: simple agent and multi-agent vs a chat
cards.b: Simple agent ~4×. Multi-agent ~15×. That is why they are only justified on high-value tasks.

cards.f: The synthesis subagent returns reports with no detail. Most likely cause?
cards.b: The coordinator did not include the previous findings in its prompt. Since it inherits no context, it is writing blind.

cards.f: Canonical definition of workflow and of agent
cards.b:
Workflow: LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths.
Agent: the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use.

cards.f: Parallelization vs orchestrator-workers: what is the real difference?
cards.b: Whether the subtasks were defined before starting. In parallelization they were; in orchestrator-workers the model decides them at runtime. It is not how many agents there are or whether they run at once.

cards.f: When does evaluator-optimizer fit?
cards.b: When there are clear evaluation criteria and feedback demonstrably improves the result. Without articulable criteria, the loop spins without converging.

cards.f: Before building an agent, what do the docs recommend trying?
cards.b: Optimizing a single call with retrieval and in-context examples. Add complexity only when it demonstrably improves the result.

cards.f: What is context rot?
cards.b: The more tokens in the window, the lower the recall accuracy. Cause: quadratic attention and training biased toward short sequences. It is a gradient, not a cliff: it fits in the window and still performs worse.

cards.f: The three techniques for long tasks, and when to use each
cards.b:
Compaction: conversational flow with lots of back and forth.
Note-taking: iterative development with clear milestones.
Multi-agent: research with parallel exploration.

cards.f: What does compaction preserve and what does it discard?
cards.b:
Preserves: architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, implementation details.
Discards: redundant tool outputs.

cards.f: Why do persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md?
cards.b: Because it is reinjected on every request. Compaction can lose the instructions from the initial prompt.

cards.f: What is the safest, lightest form of compaction?
cards.b: Tool result pruning (clearing). Once a tool was called long ago, the agent does not need to see its raw result again.

cards.f: Just-in-time vs monolithic context: what does Claude Code do?
cards.b: A hybrid: CLAUDE.md is preloaded, glob and grep retrieve just-in-time. Acknowledged trade-off: runtime exploration is slower than precomputed retrieval.

cards.f: There are user and project CLAUDE.md files with different rules. What happens?
cards.b: They are concatenated, not overwritten. That is why contradictory instructions across levels must be removed, not left to a supposed winner.

cards.f: In what order are permission rules evaluated?
cards.b: deny → ask → allow. The first match decides, and specificity does not alter that order.

cards.f: Settings precedence in Claude Code
cards.b: Managed (not overridable) → CLI arguments → local → project → user. Permission rules merge across scopes.

cards.f: Which hook guarantees a destructive action is not executed?
cards.b: PreToolUse returning a deny decision: it runs before execution. PostToolUse is too late by definition.

cards.f: Do hooks consume context window?
cards.b: No. They run in your process, outside the context window. Only whatever they choose to return consumes context.

cards.f: continue vs resume vs fork
cards.b:
continue: the most recent session in the directory, no ID.
resume: a specific session by ID.
fork: a new session with a copy of the history, leaving the original intact.

cards.f: What exactly does a session fork branch?
cards.b: The conversation, not the filesystem. File edits made in the fork are real and visible to other sessions.

cards.f: In MCP, who controls tools, resources and prompts?
cards.b:
Tools → the model.
Resources → the application (read-only).
Prompts → the user (often as slash commands).

cards.f: The two standard MCP transports
cards.b: stdio (newline-delimited JSON-RPC over a subprocess launched by the client) and Streamable HTTP (POST to a single endpoint, JSON response or SSE stream).

cards.f: Should a stdio MCP server use OAuth?
cards.b: No. The spec says stdio should not use the authorization flow: it takes credentials from the environment. OAuth applies to HTTP transports.

cards.f: Where does the token travel in a remote MCP?
cards.b: In the Authorization: Bearer header. Never in a query string. PKCE is mandatory.

cards.f: 401 vs 403 in MCP
cards.b: 401: unauthorized or invalid token. 403: insufficient scopes. 400: malformed request.

cards.f: The three MCP scopes in Claude Code
cards.b: local (per machine, default) · project (.mcp.json versioned in the repo, needs approval the first time) · user (all your projects). Precedence local > project > user.

cards.f: Does Anthropic audit the security of MCP servers?
cards.b: No. It reviews connectors against its listing criteria, but does not audit or manage the security of any server. What you expose is your responsibility.

cards.f: MCP vs Skill, in the official phrasing
cards.b: «MCP gives Claude tools for an external system, with connection and authentication handled by the server. Skills give it knowledge about how to use those tools». They are complementary.

cards.f: Hook vs instruction in CLAUDE.md or a skill: what is the criterion?
cards.b: Determinism. «Never edit .env» in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee. A PreToolUse hook that blocks is enforcement.

cards.f: Context cost of CLAUDE.md, Skills, MCP, subagents and hooks
cards.b:
CLAUDE.md: all of it, on every request.
Skills: only descriptions up front.
MCP: names up front, schemas deferred.
Subagents: isolated context.
Hooks: zero.

cards.f: The three progressive disclosure levels of a Skill
cards.b:
L1 metadata (name + description, always loaded, ~100 tokens).
L2 the body of SKILL.md, on activation.
L3 resource files, zero cost until read.

cards.f: Mandatory frontmatter of a Skill in the standard
cards.b: Only name and description. The description: max. 1024 characters, in third person, and must say what it does and when to use it.

cards.f: Where does the system prompt go in the Messages API?
cards.b: In the top-level system parameter. The messages array only accepts user and assistant: there is no system role.

429: your rate limit (also triggered by sharp traffic spikes → ramp up gradually).
529: global API overload, not yours → exponential backoff.

cards.f: In streaming, how do errors arrive?
cards.b: As event: error after an HTTP 200: the header was already sent. A handler that only looks at the status code never sees them.

cards.f: Message Batches API discount
cards.b: 50% on input and output. It stacks with prompt caching.

cards.f: Batch limits and window
cards.b: 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first. Most finish in under 1 h; results on completion or at 24 h. They expire if they do not complete within 24 h. Downloadable for 29 days.

cards.f: Does the Batch API support streaming?
cards.b: No. stream: true is not supported. Progress is tracked through the batch status counters.

cards.f: Timeout of non-streaming calls
cards.b: 10 minutes. For long operations: streaming, or Batch if latency is tolerable.

cards.f: Default retries in the official SDKs
cards.b: 2, with exponential backoff and respecting the retry-after header.

cards.f: The model selection criterion the exam expects
cards.b: Match the model to the task. Never «always use the most capable one». Haiku for volume and speed, Sonnet for balance, Opus for complex reasoning and long agentic work.

cards.f: How are reasoning tokens billed?
cards.b: As output, and they count against max_tokens, even though the text is not returned. You are charged for the tokens generated, not those of the visible summary.

cards.f: Default effort level, and its trap
cards.b: Default high. It is rendered into the prompt, so changing it between requests breaks the cached prefix. In long sessions, keep it constant.

cards.f: Do cache reads count toward the input-per-minute limit?
cards.b: No. ITPM counts input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens; cache_read_input_tokens does not count on most models.

cards.f: Does max_tokens affect the output-per-minute limit?
cards.b: No. OTPM counts the tokens actually generated, not the ceiling you requested.

cards.f: Prompt cache TTL
cards.b: 5 minutes by default, 1 hour extended. Measured from the start of the request, and every use refreshes it at no extra cost.

cards.f: Cost of writing and reading cache, and when it pays off
cards.b:
Write 1.25× (5 min) or 2× (1 h). Read 0.1×.
→ With 5 min it pays off on the first read; with 1 h, on the second.

cards.f: What invalidates the whole cache?
cards.b: Changing the tools. The prefix hierarchy is tools → system → messages, so touching tools drops everything below.

cards.f: You mark a block for caching, no error, and the cache counters are zero. What is going on?
cards.b: The block does not reach the model's minimum cacheable tokens (between 512 and 4,096 depending on the model). Below that it is not cached and no error is returned.

cards.f: Maximum number of cache breakpoints
cards.b: 4. The automatic breakpoint uses one of those four.

cards.f: What guarantees the JSON matches the schema?
cards.b: Structured outputs with constrained decoding. Always valid JSON, no retries.

cards.f: Does prefilling with { to force JSON still work?
cards.b: No. It is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later, and it is incompatible with JSON outputs. Today it is a historical distractor.

cards.f: With a strict schema, when can you still get something that does not validate?
cards.b: With stop_reason: refusal (returns 200 and the refusal prevails) and with stop_reason: max_tokens (truncated). That is why defensive validation is still mandatory.

cards.f: Is the casing of enum values guaranteed?
cards.b: No. Compare case-insensitively and avoid enums that differ only in casing.

cards.f: Without a schema, what gives more format consistency?
cards.b: Constraining with examples. The docs say it is more effective than abstract instructions.

cards.f: 20 hand-graded cases or 200 with automated grading?
cards.b: 200. Literally: «more questions with slightly worse signal and automated grading is better than fewer questions hand-graded at high quality».

cards.f: Preference order of grading methods
cards.b: Code (exact/string match) → LLM-as-judge → human. On human grading the docs say literally «Avoid if possible».

cards.f: Three rules for a reliable LLM-as-judge
cards.b:
1) Detailed, clear rubric.
2) Bounded output: binary or a 1-5 scale.
3) Ask it to reason before scoring and then discard the reasoning.

cards.f: How do you tell a hallucination from a prompt failure in production?
cards.b: Repeat the same input several times (best-of-N). Inconsistent → hallucination. Reproducible → prompt or model capability.

cards.f: Grounding technique for long documents
cards.b: Ask for the relevant verbatim quotes before answering (for documents over 20k tokens), and retract any claim that has no quote backing it.

cards.f: Official example of a well-formulated success criterion
cards.b: «Fewer than 0.1% of outputs over 10,000 trials flagged by the content filter». The bad one would be «safe outputs»: specific and measurable vs vague.

cards.f: Where should untrusted content go?
cards.b: Only in tool_result blocks, never in the system prompt or in user text. Claude is trained to treat instructions appearing there with skepticism.

cards.f: Why JSON-encode untrusted content?
cards.b: Escaping gives unambiguous delimiters and prevents «escaping» the context by closing quotes or tags.

cards.f: An agent has tools it does not need. What is the right answer?
cards.b: Remove the capability. Logging is forensic, confirming suffers approval fatigue, and instructing in the prompt is a request. None of the three closes the vector.

cards.f: Can you put your own instructions inside a tool_result?
cards.b: No. They are ignored or flagged as injection. They go in a later user turn.

cards.f: Can an API key's expiry be changed after it is created?
cards.b: No. It is chosen at creation time and cannot be modified. After expiry: 401, and they are not reactivated.

cards.f: Does CORS work with zero data retention?
cards.b: Not supported. You must route through a backend proxy: never call the API from the browser.

cards.f: When do you NOT need to build RAG?
cards.b: If the knowledge base fits under ~200,000 tokens (~500 pages): put it all in the prompt. With prompt caching, latency >2× lower and cost up to 90% lower.

cards.f: Why add BM25 to vector search?
cards.b: Embeddings miss exact lexical matches — identifiers, error codes, rare names. Official example: «Error code TS-999». They are combined with rank fusion.

cards.f: Contextual retrieval figures (failure reduction)
cards.b: Contextual embeddings alone −35% · + contextual BM25 −49% · + reranking −67%. The benefits stack.

cards.f: Reranking: how many results are retrieved and how many reach the model?
cards.b: Retrieve top-150, rerank and pass top-20. Top-20 performs better than top-10 and top-5.

cards.f: Two RAG approaches Anthropic tested and discarded
cards.b: Generic document summaries added to each chunk («very limited gains») and summary-based indexing («poor performance»). They sound reasonable: they are perfect distractors.

cards.f: HIPAA vs ZDR with a non-eligible feature
cards.b:
Under HIPAA the API blocks with a 400.
Under ZDR the API does not block: using it is opting out of the agreement for that specific data.

cards.f: At what level does HIPAA apply, and can it be turned off?
cards.b: At the organization level, and once enabled it is permanent: an admin cannot turn it off. For HIPAA and non-HIPAA workloads you need separate organizations.

cards.f: Under HIPAA, where must PHI never appear?
cards.b: In JSON schema definitions: property names, enum, const, pattern. Schemas are cached separately and do not get the protections.

cards.f: Three features not eligible for zero data retention
cards.b: Batch processing (retains results), Files API and code execution. Also the MCP connector and CORS.

cards.f: Claude cites a specific article number from a regulation. What do you do?
cards.b: Verify it against the official text before sharing. Precise-looking details are exactly where it hallucinates, and self-declared confidence is not a signal of accuracy.

cards.f: You are asked to analyze an Excel file with names and account numbers
cards.b: Anonymize or remove the identifiers before uploading it. Internal use does not exempt you from the policy, and «instructing the model not to retain» is not a compliance control.

cards.f: «Automate this 6-step manual process with Claude»
cards.b: Analyze the process before automating it. Two steps may be unnecessary and only one may deserve AI. Automating a bad process gives you a faster bad process.

cards.f: You always fix the same thing by hand in every output. What does that mean?
cards.b: That fix is configuration, not work. Move it into the Project instructions so it comes out right the first time.

cards.f: A Project that worked degrades after six months. Typical cause?
cards.b: The knowledge sources and instructions went stale and nobody maintained them. A Project is a living artifact.

cards.f: Is extended thinking with budget_tokens still current?
cards.b: No. Deprecated and rejected with 400 on recent models. Today adaptive thinking rules, on by default.

cards.f: Are sampling and roots still alive in MCP?
cards.b: No. Deprecated in the current spec. The live client primitive is elicitation, and the modern spec is stateless (no initialize handshake).

cards.f: Is Task or Agent the subagent tool?
cards.b: The exam guide says Task; current docs renamed it to Agent and both coexist in recent releases. On the exam, anchor your answer in the guide.

cards.f: At what level does the stop_reason tool_use / end_turn pair live?
cards.b: At the Messages API level. In the Agent SDK result tool_use is not a possible value, because the SDK loop does not stop there.

cards.f: You port an agent from claude -p to the Agent SDK and it loses tone and conventions. Why?
cards.b: The CLI uses the full prompt by default; the Agent SDK starts with a minimal prompt covering only tool calling. Set the preset explicitly when porting.

cards.f: You send tools in the request. What does the API add to your system prompt?
cards.b: A block of tool use instructions plus the JSON schemas, before yours. Hundreds of tokens you didn't write, and they vary with tool_choice.

cards.f: A prompt works well on claude.ai and differently via API. Cause?
cards.b: claude.ai applies its own product system prompt (date, format, behavior) that does not exist in the API. Anthropic publishes it in their release notes.

cards.f: Long context: where does the question go and where the documents?
cards.b: Documents at the top, question at the end. In 20k+ token contexts the docs report up to 30% better quality.

cards.f: Structured output complexity limits per request
cards.b: 20 tools with strict · 24 optional parameters total · 16 with union types · compilation timeout 180 s.

cards.f: "Schema is too complex for compilation". First lever?
cards.b: Turn optionals into required: each optional nearly doubles part of the state space. Then: flatten nesting and split across several requests.

cards.f: Which JSON Schema constraints does strict mode NOT support?
cards.b: Numeric constraints (minimum/maximum), string length, recursive schemas and external $ref. They 400: validate ranges in your code.

cards.f: You've corrected Claude twice on the same thing and it's getting worse
cards.b: The context is polluted with failed approaches. Official heuristic: clear it and restate more precisely, don't push on in the same thread.

cards.f: What is lost in a compaction and what survives?
cards.b:
Survives: system prompt, root CLAUDE.md and automatic memory (re-injected from disk).
Lost: rules with paths: and nested CLAUDE.md, until a file that activates them is read again.

cards.f: The four install scopes of a plugin
cards.b: user (default) · project (versioned in the repo, travels with git) · local (gitignored) · managed (read-only, not overridable).

cards.f: What determines whether a plugin updates?
cards.b: Its version, which is the cache key. Cascade: manifest → marketplace entry → commit SHA → digest → unknown.

cards.f: The five platforms and who processes the data
cards.b: Claude API → Anthropic · Bedrock → AWS · Claude Platform on AWS → Anthropic · Google Cloud → Google · Foundry → Anthropic on Azure.

cards.f: Client requires FedRAMP High and AWS as the sole processor
cards.b: Claude on Amazon Bedrock. That's the rule the docs publish. Watch the distractor: Claude Platform on AWS runs on AWS but the processor is Anthropic.

cards.f: Two format differences of Vertex versus the 1P API
cards.b: model does not go in the body (it goes in the URL) and anthropic_version does go in the body (not as a header).

cards.f: On Bedrock, invoking a new model with its base ID gives 400. Why?
cards.b: It requires an inference profile: region prefix (global., us., eu.) or the profile ARN. Regional routing guarantees residency at +10% price.

cards.f: Where does the Message Batches API exist?
cards.b: Only in the Claude API and in Claude Platform on AWS. Not Bedrock, not Vertex, not Foundry. Same for data residency.

cards.f: What has to change in the code when migrating provider?
cards.b: Only the client class and authentication. The messages call is identical. What does change a lot is feature availability.

cards.f: Strands, LangGraph and PydanticAI: what's the axis of each?
cards.b:
Strands: model-driven loop already built, AWS-first deployment.
LangGraph: orchestration by state graph, durability and human-in-the-loop.
PydanticAI: typed loop, the data contract rules.

cards.f: LangGraph: checkpointer vs store
cards.b:
Checkpointer: snapshots of one thread's state, short-term memory, time travel.
Store: key-value across threads, long-term memory.

cards.f: Why must nodes be idempotent with checkpointing?
cards.b: Checkpoints are saved at step boundaries, not mid-node: on resume, the node re-runs in full. If it charged a payment, it charges again.

cards.f: Anthropic's documented stance on frameworks
cards.b: "The most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks". Start by calling the API directly; if you use a framework, understand what's underneath.

cards.f: Agent SDK vs Managed Agents
cards.b:
Agent SDK: loop built, runs in your process.
Managed Agents: hosted harness with REST API for long, async agents. They are different products.

cards.f: Is Managed Agents eligible for ZDR or HIPAA BAA?
cards.b: No. It is stateful by design: it persists session history server-side. Per-session isolation exists, but compliance eligibility runs on another track.

cards.f: You self-host the Agent SDK and threads are lost on restart
cards.b: The SDK spawns one subprocess per session with transcripts on local disk, which doesn't survive a restart. Production needs an external session store.

cards.f: The output doesn't have the expected shape
cards.b: An output constraint is missing. Rewording the instruction won't fix it: it's not a wording problem.

cards.f: The agent drifts in tone and judgement across turns
cards.b: Underspecified system prompt. Neither examples nor schema fix drift: they target other symptoms.

cards.f: The content is right but it invents the structure
cards.b: Missing few-shot examples to pin it down.

cards.f: You've iterated the prompt and unforeseen inputs still break it
cards.b: Leave the prompt: structured output in the API. JSON outputs constrains the final response; strict tool use validates tool arguments. Cost: compilation on the first call plus input tokens.

cards.f: Tool selection degrades from turn N onward
cards.b: Look at the context window, not the schema. If it failed from the first turn, then it would indeed be the description.

cards.f: Tool use error when retrying after a dropped stream
cards.b: A half-built block, not the schema. A block is only closed at its content_block_stop.

cards.f: Two tools get confused even though their schemas don't look alike
cards.b: Claude chooses by reading the description, not the schema. Add the exclusion condition: one line saying when NOT to call it.

cards.f: How large are real tool outputs versus development fixtures?
cards.b: 3 to 5 times larger. A session that holds 50 turns in testing can hit the ceiling at turn 8 in production.

cards.f: Context cost of connecting five MCP servers "just in case"
cards.b: ~55,000 tokens in definitions before Claude does anything. Tool search cuts it by over 85%; it defers the context, not the payload.

cards.f: A stream cuts off mid tool_use block. What can you NOT do?
cards.b: Rebuild it from the partial deltas. Tool use and thinking blocks are not partially recoverable; you only resume from the last text block.

cards.f: When is a block closed and when does a message end?
cards.b: The block, at its content_block_stop. The message, at message_stop. A tool use's deltas are partial JSON: don't parse before the block closes.

cards.f: Formula for the cost of an image
cards.b: ⌈width/28⌉ × ⌈height/28⌉ visual tokens. Claude sees 28×28 px patches, not pixels.

cards.f: Visual token ceiling per image
cards.b: It goes by tier, not by model. High resolution (4.7+): max side 2576 px, 4784 tokens. Standard: 1568 px and 1568 tokens. Anything larger is rescaled automatically.

cards.f: Inline base64, Files API or Batches: when each?
cards.b: base64: single-use image. Files API: assets reused across requests (avoids resending bytes every turn). Batches: offline work, lower cost per token, non-deterministic latency.

cards.f: Is firing a thousand synchronous calls in parallel batching?
cards.b: No. Parallelism doesn't lower cost per token. It's the mistake the material names explicitly.

cards.f: The four memory scopes and what decides which one
cards.b: The shape of the session decides. In context (easy, fails sooner) · external (latency, survives) · summarized (cheap, loses what isn't preserved) · stateless (jobs that close).

cards.f: Repeatable state vs repeatable instructions
cards.b: Different problems. State is memory. Repeatable instructions are a Skill: markdown loaded on demand when its description matches, not injected into every session.

cards.f: Workflow or agent, in one sentence
cards.b: Workflow if you can write the exact steps in code. Agent if you can specify the goal and the tools but not the path.

cards.f: A tool can do something irreversible. When does the human checkpoint come in?
cards.b: Before wiring the loop, as a design decision. After the first incident the write already reached the customer. A log is forensic, not preventive.

cards.f: When to turn on reasoning?
cards.b: Only where a reasoning pass changes the answer, calibrating effort to the problem instead of raising it on every call. Thinking blocks come back unmodified or the next request fails.

cards.f: By what criterion is the permission mode chosen?
cards.b: By the risk profile of the work and the environment, not by a preference for fewer prompts. Bypass against a live repository removes every control point.

cards.f: The permission mode isn't enough to protect a critical path. What do you add?
cards.b: A deny rule on that path, at project or enterprise level. The mode decides how much it asks; the rule decides what is unreachable.

cards.f: An automated reviewer says: a null check is missing on line 40, and this will degrade the payments service
cards.b: The first is provable from the diff: confirm it on the cited line. The second is a hypothesis to verify: it asserted it without the evidence that would prove it.

cards.f: Where does the human gate go in an automated review?
cards.b: Where a finding turns into an action that's hard to reverse. Not on every comment (noise and rubber-stamping) nor at the end (the damage is done).

cards.f: Too many false positives in the CI review
cards.b: Give it the team's conventions, otherwise it has to guess. Asking for more rigor without criteria increases the noise.

cards.f: The four durable-context mechanisms and what each one solves
cards.b:
CLAUDE.md: project memory, dilutes with size.
Rule files: scope guidance to where it applies.
Hooks: enforce deterministically.
Subagents: move exploration out of the main context.

cards.f: What happens if you put all four mechanisms in a single CLAUDE.md?
cards.b: A file that dilutes, costs more to maintain and is easier to ignore. Each mechanism solves a different problem.

cards.f: Your plugin installs on your machine and fails on everyone else's
cards.b: Almost certainly an absolute path to your home directory. Rules: paths relative to the project root, environment variables documented or validated at install, and test from a clean machine.

cards.f: What makes a skill portable across Claude Code, API and Agent SDK?
cards.b: A scoped description and no assumptions about the local environment. Each runtime loads it differently: filesystem, beta headers with container, and setting sources.

cards.f: Do subagents preload the main thread's skills?
cards.b: No, in any runtime. They start clean. If they need a specific skill, declare it in their definition.

cards.f: stdio or HTTP: what decides which?
cards.b: stdio for servers running on your machine. HTTP for anything hosted remotely or used by several developers.

cards.f: A stdio server declared in the repo's .mcp.json
cards.b: A configuration that looks shareable and isn't: the file travels with the repo, but the process only exists on the machine of whoever wrote it.

cards.f: What does a team MCP server require?
cards.b: HTTP transport and project or enterprise scope, both. Transport and scope are independent decisions with dependent consequences.

cards.f: Regulated client: identity, credentials, auditing and configuration control
cards.b: Identity → OAuth. Service credentials → environment variables. Auditing → PostToolUse hooks. Configuration lockdown → enterprise managed settings.

cards.f: Why does identifying security requirements before deploying matter?
cards.b: None of the four controls is hard to implement, but all are hard to retrofit after a deployment has failed a security review.

cards.f: When do you write the eval?
cards.b: Before building. Identifying the expected behavior forces you to define success while the design can still change. It turns "it's done" from a feeling into a score.

cards.f: Grader by the shape of the output
cards.b: A single correct form → exact match. Structured output → code check. Open-ended quality → LLM judge, calibrated beforehand against human-labeled cases.

cards.f: Unit and functional green, e2e red
cards.b: The break is at the seam between components. Full answer in two halves: fix the handoff and add the integration test that was missing.

cards.f: What does each test level catch?
cards.b: Unit: logic inside one component. Functional: that it meets its spec. Integration: the handoff between two. E2E: the whole flow — it says it fails, not where.

cards.f: What is a trace for?
cards.b: To know which step produced the bad result. It turns a day of investigation into a short fix.

cards.f: One search or iterative search?
cards.b: A single one for single-fact queries. Iterative when the question is genuinely multi-step. Iterating on something simple burns tokens without improving anything.

cards.f: First question for any failure
cards.b: Could waiting and retrying fix it? If yes → exponential backoff with a cap and a budget. Never an immediate loop, which only makes it worse.

cards.f: A failure no retry fixes
cards.b: Demands a named fallback. Without one, the unhandled exception becomes the default behavior and one bad response takes down the whole flow.

cards.f: A tool fails: empty result or error flag?
cards.b: Error flag. The model reads empty as valid data and reasons about something that doesn't exist.

cards.f: Cost has spiked and you don't know where
cards.b: Instrument first: token cost, latency and error rate on every call. Then tune one chosen lever, instead of guessing from the invoice.

cards.f: When does the orchestrator-workers pattern earn its cost?
cards.b: Only on tasks that split into independent parallel parts. It multiplies cost by the number of subagents (~15× in the published case); on coupled work a single agent does it for a fraction.

cards.f: "Our users are trusted, injection doesn't affect us"
cards.b: Doesn't help: injection arrives through the content the agent reads, not the user who types. The model reads its whole context as a single token stream, with no line between instruction and data.

cards.f: What gives a regulated reviewer control over the action boundary?
cards.b: A hook that blocks and logs before the tool runs. "Before" is what makes it a control; a later log only allows inspection.

cards.f: What unit should you think and budget in?
cards.b: In tokens, not words. It's what the API measures and charges, and what the context window measures. The word-token conversion isn't constant.

cards.f: The two ways to break the context window
cards.b:
The input doesn't fit → error before generating, no partial response.
It runs out midway → truncated output with stop_reason: model_context_window_exceeded.

cards.f: Who manages the conversation history?
cards.b: The application. The window is a fixed budget that holds the entire request at once; nobody prunes for you.

cards.f: Why does a test that compares against exact text fail?
cards.b: Sampling makes generation non-deterministic: the same prompt returns different wording. That's what evals exist for.

cards.f: Model and reasoning mode: how are they chosen?
cards.b: They are separate, composable levers. Floor-up rule: the smallest model and the simplest reasoning that pass your eval, adding capacity only where the eval asks for it.

cards.f: The four interaction modes and what decides them
cards.b: Synchronous · streaming · async/await · batch. Two questions: is anyone waiting? and real time or offline volume?

cards.f: Does streaming speed up the response?
cards.b: No. It improves perceived latency, in exchange for you assembling the response from partial events.

cards.f: Alias or pinned model version?
cards.b: Pin the specific version, and keep the previous one available. An alias is "the current edition of the book": the text changes without notice. With a pin, you adopt the change deliberately and have a way back.

cards.f: How do you choose and defend a deployment platform?
cards.b: You choose by the client's cloud and compliance posture. You defend it by measuring: latency from their region, compliance against their certification, and total cost per call, not price per token.

cards.f: When is compliance raised with a regulated client?
cards.b: At scoping. It's pass or fail: if it shows up late, it kills the build at contract review.

cards.f: What does a well-packaged accelerator keep and what does it expose?
cards.b: It keeps the reusable logic, exposes the client-specific parts as documented parameters, and ships the eval and the audit log. Package while hot: knowing what was client-specific is the most expensive thing to reconstruct later.

cards.f: What does a maintainer accept?
cards.b: What they can verify: scoped code, a runnable example, a test and the assumptions written down. License rights are confirmed before the technical review.

cards.f: Is trust inherited between components?
cards.b: No. Every point where data crosses is a trust boundary and must be established explicitly. An application is only as contained as its most privileged seam.

cards.f: A seam that can't be secured
cards.b: Goes to a human owner, it doesn't ship.
